title: The Problem with Temporal Distance, as Illustrated by Bryan et al Prosocial Intervention
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart explains why he took down a chart correlating education with long-term earnings that used to hang in his classroom: research shows humans, and especially adolescents, are poor temporal reasoners who irrationally discount rewards that are far off in time. He cites a Bryan et al. study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in which eighth graders were split into two groups — one taught that junk food harms future health (a temporally distant, utility-based appeal), the other taught about manipulative food-industry marketing practices (a temporally proximate, justice/autonomy-based appeal). The group given the industry-critique framing made healthier food choices the next day, while the future-health framing had little effect. Stuart draws the direct classroom implication: "you'll need this in the real world" arguments are weak precisely because they rely on temporally distant payoffs, and teachers should instead diversify their appeals across his "Rainbow of Why" — including proximate motivators like autonomy and justice — rather than leaning on utility alone.
points: Stuart grounds a classroom practice change (removing a career-earnings poster) in a specific empirical finding: adolescents are especially poor at valuing temporally distant rewards, making long-term payoff arguments a weak motivational lever.

The Bryan et al. study he cites shows an autonomy-and-justice framing (exposing food industry manipulation) outperformed a future-health framing for changing eighth graders' actual next-day food choices — a real behavioral outcome, not just a stated preference.

"You'll need this in the real world" arguments are named as a common but weak teacher move precisely because they're temporally distant utility claims, the exact category the cited research shows students discount most heavily.
The prescribed fix is diversifying motivational appeals across the full "Rainbow of Why" (autonomy, justice, enjoyment, etc.), not abandoning value-based arguments altogether.
quotes: But I've kept the poster down for a more fundamental reason. And the reason is this: human beings are bad temporal reasoners.
In one of my favorite papers on the Value belief, Bryan et al. put it this way: People discount the value of temporally distant rewards to an extreme and irrational degree.
This is why I basically never make arguments to my students about what they'll need in the "real world." First of all, this is disparaging toward both school and student lives.

Group A was taught that unhealthy food is bad for your future health. Group B was taught about the manipulative and unfair practices of the food industry (e.g., engineering junk food to be addictive and marketing it to young children).

Basically, students weren't as motivated by the temporally distant rewards of healthy eating as they were by the temporally proximate reward of doing their part to "stick it to the man" and resist the food industry.

Temporally distant claims (e.g., "You'll use this in the real world;" "You'll need this someday") are plays at utility, and they have limited power, in part because humans are bad at temporal wisdom and in part because utility is way overused in school.

Whereas what the researchers did for Group B angled at things like autonomy — students were given information but not told what they should do — and justice — in this case, by highlighting the injustices of some junk food industry practices.
